scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for a parent to force their 13-year-old son to play sports or participate in some extracurricular activity because the son is really lazy. The parent is frustrated because the son gets poor grades, doesn't take care of himself, and seems uninterested in doing anything productive. The mother, who shares custody, isn't pushing him and is enabling his behavior. The parent wants to snap him out of this by making him join a team sport, thinking that being around peers who are working hard and having fun might give him the push he needs. The parent is considering making him play basketball for a season, allowing him to quit after that if he doesn't like it. The question is, would that make the parent a jerk, or is it a morally acceptable action? First, I need to understand the situation better. The son is 13, which is a pre-teen/teenage age where independence is starting to kick in, but he's still young enough that parental guidance is crucial. The son's behavior includes laziness, poor hygiene, lack of responsibility, and poor academic performance. The parent's intention is to help the son develop a work ethic and better habits by involving him in an extracurricular activity. Now, considering the parent's perspective, they're trying to intervene because the current environment isn't fostering positive growth. The mother's approach is enabling, which might be contributing to the son's behavior. The parent wants to take a more active role to help the son improve. On the other hand, forcing a child into an activity they don't want to participate in could have negative consequences. It might lead to resentment, resistance, or even more defiance. The child might feel that his autonomy is being taken away, which could harm the parent-child relationship. However, the parent is considering allowing the son to quit after a season if he doesn't like it, which shows some consideration for the son's feelings and preferences. It's a compromise between forcing him to participate and giving him some control over the situation. I also need to think about the potential benefits of extracurricular activities. Participation in sports or other team-oriented activities can teach discipline, teamwork, responsibility, and time management. These are valuable life skills that could help the son in the long run. Additionally, being part of a team might encourage him to socialize more positively and build friendships based on shared interests and goals. But there's also the risk that the son might not enjoy the activity, leading to further disengagement. The parent needs to ensure that the activity is something the son might at least be somewhat interested in, or that it's a good fit for his personality and abilities. Another aspect to consider is the parent's own behavior. Forcing the son into an activity could be seen as controlling or overbearing, which might not be the best approach to parenting. It's important to balance guidance with allowing the child to make his own choices, even if those choices aren't ideal in the parent's eyes. Perhaps a better approach would be to have a conversation with the son about the importance of being active, responsible, and having a work ethic. The parent could explain their concerns and the reasons behind wanting him to participate in an extracurricular activity. This way, the son feels heard and understood, and the parent is fostering open communication. Setting boundaries and expectations is also crucial. The parent could establish that participation in an activity is a requirement, but allow the son to choose which one, giving him some control over the situation. This might make him more willing to engage and less likely to resist. In summary, while the parent's intention is to help the son develop positive habits and a work ethic, forcing him into an activity without considering his feelings and preferences could be counterproductive. It's important to approach the situation with empathy, open communication, and a willingness to compromise to find a solution that works for both the parent and the child.
